transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-02-14 16:00 PST | Duration: ~42 minutes | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Tom (Redwood SE), Jenna (Aegis Head of ML), Marcus (Platform Eng), Sofia (Security), Trevor (Product)

Summary: quick intros, current stack, integration questions on SDKs and infra, security requirements, and pilot plan.

00:00 Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood, i'll hand over to priya to do a quick intro on integration paths
00:18 Priya: hi all, priya shah, solutions engineer at Redwood. high level we support hosted api, dedicated reserved pools and private vpc/on-prem deployments. today i'd like to focus on how you'd integrate SDKs (langchain/llamaindex), options for a gateway or proxy, and observability hooks you asked about
00:34 Jenna: thanks priya. we run a hybrid infra model, most inference right now is hosted with another vendor but we're exploring dedicated for lower latency and private for data residency. main ask is easy integration into our retrieval stack which is built on langchain and a couple of in-house wrappers
00:51 Marcus: yep, we have a k8s cluster for model ops and a proxy layer in front for rate limiting. curious about how Redwood's gateway would fit or if we keep our existing gateway and just proxy calls to Redwood
01:10 Priya: good question. two common patterns: 1) customers keep their gateway/proxy and call Redwood's hosted API directly (we recommend using our SDK for retry/backoff), or 2) route through a small sidecar proxy to add auth, telemetry and custom quotas before hitting Redwood. both supported. for dedicated you can host a customer-facing gateway in your vpc that talks to the dedicated pool over private peering
01:32 Trevor: is that traffic encrypted end-to-end? we need to satisfy internal security for PII in prompts
01:40 Priya: yes TLS in transit. for private/deployed we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations for key wrapping. also audit logs and per-request IDs in the console. note: there's an auto-audit export we can enable for SOC2 outputs
01:55 Sofia: about retention - does Redwood store prompts by default on Hosted? how long and is there a way to disable retention for sensitive inputs
02:05 Alex: hosted has configurable retention, default is short, and we have a no-retention option for enterprise. for dedicated/private you control storage and logs which helps with compliance
02:18 Marcus: helps. technical: priya, can you talk about SDK support for langchain and llamain—llama index?
02:26 Priya: sure. we provide official SDKs in python and node, plus example connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex. examples include chains for retrieval-augmented generation, and a small wrapper that handles token accounting. i'll send the repo link after the call. note sometimes community examples use 'llamaidx' and names vary so watch for mismatched imports.
02:50 Jenna: do you have streaming support? we need partial responses for our chat flows
02:55 Priya: yes streaming via websocket or http chunked responses; our python SDK exposes an async stream iterator. streaming works on hosted and dedicated. private on-prem supports streaming but requires a little extra config to open persistent connections through the gateway
03:12 Marcus: about rate limits — we have variable QPS, spikes during promotions. how are quotas applied and can we burst above baseline?
03:22 Priya: we have per-account and per-route quotas. dedicated allows you to reserve capacity for steady-state and configure burst capacity. hosted has token-based quotas and throttles — you can request increased burst windows. for very spiky workloads we recommend dedicated with autoscaling + burst pools or using our prefix KV cache to cut token usage
03:44 Marcus: what's the latency hit for the KV/prefix cache? we need 95th < 120ms for short prompts
03:52 Tom: caching reduces token generation cost and often lowers tail latency because the model can reuse KV cache; but latency depends on sequence length and model. for short prompts we've seen good 95th p95 numbers on dedicated with optimized kernels. we can run benchmarks against your sample traffic to confirm.
04:12 Jenna: that would be useful. can we run a small pilot for 2 weeks? compare hosted vs dedicated with same model and traffic patterns
04:20 Alex: absolutely — pilot is common. typical workflow: share SDK examples + prompts, you run a small load or we run with Redwood-managed harness, collect traces and token-level cost, then review. we'll provide a pilot plan and success criteria
04:36 Trevor: observability — what hooks do you provide? we want trace correlation between our request id and the model's tokens and latency
04:44 Priya: we emit request-level traces and metadata. options: 1) inject your request_id as a header and it surfaces in our logs and trace ids, 2) OpenTelemetry export (OTel) to your collector, 3) webhook/event stream for token-level billing events. our Console exposes per-route token cost and latency breakouts. note sometimes product docs call it 'redwood console' or 'RCon' in old notes
05:10 Sofia: are traces sampled? we need full fidelity for a subset of requests for debugging
05:16 Priya: by default we sample but you can opt into full tracing for pilot or dedicated pools — there's a storage/retention cost tradeoff. we can enable 100% for the pilot for a specific route ID
05:30 Marcus: about auth — do you support SSO/SSO, SAML? api keys?
05:36 Alex: we support API keys, SAML SSO for the Console, and for dedicated/private customer-managed SSO for admin plane. tokens for the runtime are scoped per-route and you can rotate via the API
05:50 Jenna: deployment timeline — if pilot is successful we want dedicated by end of Q2. is that realistic?
05:58 Alex: yes for most customers. dedicated provisioning typically takes a few days to a couple weeks depending on GPU availability and region. private/vpc on-prem is longer (4–8 weeks) because of networking and security review
06:12 Trevor: can you clarify model pinning and rollouts? we have concerns about sudden quality regressions when platforms push updated model weights
06:20 Tom: you can pin to a specific model version. Redwood supports rollouts: canary, A/B and automatic fallback to a compatible variant if latency/SLOs degrade. the Console will show per-version metrics and you can tie rollouts to prompt-set evals
06:36 Jenna: our ML lead cares about reproducibility for evals; do you support deterministic seeds for sampling?
06:42 Tom: we expose temperature/seed controls; for some model families determinism may vary but we support seeds and fixed sampling to help reproduce results for evaluations
06:54 Marcus: technical deep dive — our current stack uses langchain chains that call an internal proxy which does caching, reranking and then calls the model. what's the simplest integration path?
07:03 Priya: simplest is to swap the backend client in your proxy to call Redwood's SDK. keep your proxy for caching and pre/post-processing. another pattern is to adapt our sdk inside your chain components — we have small wrappers for LangChain LLM wrappers and retriever adapters for LlamaIndex
07:28 Jenna: any gotchas with token counting? we've seen mismatches between platform and model vendors
07:34 Priya: tokenization differences are common. we provide a token counter utility in our SDK that uses the same BPE/tokenizer as the served model. recommend using that in preflight to estimate cost. also note role tokens for chat formats can vary
07:50 Sofia: security again — KMS integration details? we use AWS KMS with strict key policies and a dedicated HSM in some regions
07:58 Alex: supported. for private/dedicated you can bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK) and we integrate with AWS KMS and external HSMs via standard key wrap. we can share the cryptographic attestation doc and KMS integration guide
08:13 Marcus: observability integration — do you export to datadog/new relic/jaeger?
08:18 Priya: yes we have exporters for DataDog and NewRelic and OTel/Jaeger collectors. the event schema includes request_id, route, model_version, tokens_in/out, latency_ms, and cost_estimate. we can share the sample payloads
08:34 Trevor: what about rate-limiting headers? can we see X-RateLimit-Remaining or similar for client-side logic
08:40 Priya: yes we surface rate limit headers and provide backoff guidance in the SDK. for high-throughput customers we also provide a token bucket view in Console so you can monitor consumption in real time
08:55 Jenna: any network egress fees in dedicated/private?
09:00 Alex: networking depends on deployment; hosted egress is typical cloud egress. dedicated in same cloud region often avoids cross-region fees; private on-prem is native in your network so no Redwood egress fees but there may be peering costs. we'll map expected costs in the pricing sheet
09:18 Marcus: for pilot we want to use our own gateway and route traffic to hosted first, compare latency and cost, then try dedicated. is that doable?
09:27 Alex: yes that's a standard approach. hosted for quick iteration, dedicated for evaluation under load, then private if data residency or KMS needs require it
09:36 Priya: i'll note two technical items for the pilot: 1) we need a representative prompt set and traffic pattern, 2) enable full tracing for route ids in pilot. priya: i'll provide sample load runner we use locally to replicate your qps
09:52 Jenna: good. do you have examples for LlamaIndex retriever adapters? ours uses a hybrid search + embedding flow
09:58 Priya: yes — we have an adapter that wraps embedding calls and caches vectors; for hybrid flows we suggest using the embedding endpoint with batching and our recommended quantization settings if you self-host the model. i'll send the example notebook
10:16 Marcus: batching — we currently batch at the proxy level. does Redwood do batching in the runtime too? how does that interact with our proxy batching?
10:24 Tom: Redwood does continuous batching on the runtime. if you batch upstream, the runtime's batching will see single-request large batches; both can be complementary but upstream batching changes latency characteristics. we'll test both during pilot
10:40 Trevor: do you have any known limitations with LangChain's async chains?
10:45 Priya: generally it's compatible; we have an async LLM wrapper that plays nicely with LangChain's Async chains. small caveats around streaming and token accounting — our wrapper addresses those.
10:59 Jenna: procurement questions — what's typical contract length for dedicated and discounts?
11:04 Alex: dedicated usually annual commitments; discounts scale with committed spend. pilot to dedicated conversion often includes pilot credit applied to first committed month. i'll provide sample contract language
11:18 Sofia: security pack — we'll need SOC2 report, pen test summary, and data flow diagram before security sign-off
11:25 Alex: noted. i'll send the security pack and ask our security team to join the next call if needed. we also have a compliance questionnaire template for you to fill
11:36 Marcus: one more: can we pin a model family but allow Redwood to apply micro-optimizations like quantization in the runtime? we don't want quality regressions from unseen quantization changes
11:46 Tom: you control quantization profiles for dedicated/private. for hosted we recommend specific quantization profiles per workload and we surface expected numeric differences. you can pin to a non-quantized variant if determinism is critical. also we have eval hooks to run prompt sets and monitor quality regressions automatically
12:05 Jenna: great. let's recap next steps
12:10 Alex: recap: Alex will send pricing and contract; Priya will share SDK examples, LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters, observability payload samples and pilot harness; Marcus will send infra diagram and traffic patterns; Sofia will send list of security docs needed. schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2028-02-20.
12:34 Jenna: thanks everyone
12:38 Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up with links and scheduling
12:42 call end
